analysis.title: Global Economics Analyst: Macro Outlook 2027: Steady Baseline, Downside Risks
key_insights: Global GDP grew 2.7% in 2026, in line with potential, as AI capex, easier financial conditions and fiscal expansion offset the Iran-war energy supply shock. GS forecasts 2.8% in 2027, 0.1pp above potential.
Global headline inflation is on course to end 2026 at 3.7% Q4/Q4, 1.3pp above GS's forecast from a year earlier, because of the Iran war.

Energy flips from a 0.4pp drag on global growth in 2026 to a modest boost in 2027. Commodity strategists' baseline has Brent at $78/bbl by end-2027, with LNG prices normalizing similarly. Europe keeps a drag from delayed energy cost pass-through.

The GS FCI has tightened about 50bp in the US and 30bp in DMs over three months on lower equity prices and higher rates, implying a moderate drag on growth over the next few quarters. The DM fiscal impulse is only slightly positive in 2027.

Japan is the main fiscal exception, with a 0.7pp boost to GDP growth from consumption tax cuts, higher defense spending and the Takaichi administration's investment plans. GS expects modestly positive impulses in Germany and the US, and a continued fiscal drag in the UK.

Global nominal AI investment is forecast to rise from $1.1tn in 2026 to $1.8tn in 2027, driven by more than $500bn of extra US hardware spending. The year-over-year change as a share of GDP peaks in 2027H1, and the level peaks in 2028.

AI investment adds 0.4pp to global GDP growth in 2027. The boost to measured US GDP is 0.2pp because of undercounting of semiconductor investment and chip-related IP exports, and the boost to 'true' US GDP is 0.6pp.

China is forecast at 4.5% growth in 2027 (consensus 4.4%), driven by exports and a wider trade surplus. Domestic demand stays weak, with a property drag of 1.3pp of GDP. China is a 0.1pp headwind to rest-of-world growth, with larger drags in Germany (-0.3pp) and Central Europe (-0.2pp).

GS is above consensus on 2027 growth for the US (2.4% vs 2.2%), South Korea (3.2% vs 2.7%) and Taiwan (6.3% vs 5.9%). It is below consensus for the Euro area (0.9% vs 1.3%) because of tighter financial conditions and higher energy prices biting this winter.

Downside risk 1 is an Iran escalation. The commodity team puts more weight on an upside scenario with oil at $132/bbl, driven by shipping attacks, infrastructure damage and a persistent risk premium. Unlike in 2026, FCI and fiscal impulses would not offset the hit.

Downside risk 2 is bond market turbulence. The DM yield curve is 85bp above early-2026 levels, which would subtract a cumulative 0.5% from GDP if sustained. Only part of this drag is in the forecast because GS expects fewer hikes than priced.

France's 10-year OAT yield is about 150bp above Germany's. GS does not expect meaningful consolidation talks until after the April 2027 presidential and June parliamentary elections, so the market could force an earlier and larger growth drag.

Downside risk 3 is a weaker AI impulse. Hyperscaler stock reactions to capex signals on earnings calls turned slightly negative in 2026 after being positive in 2024-2025, and upward capex revisions slowed in the Q3 season.

AI capex near-term risks are capacity constraints (semiconductor and memory order backlogs through 2028), credit markets ($687bn of AI-related debt and $115bn of AI-related equity issued so far in 2026, with more crowd-out possible in 2027) and regulation (possible data center permitting moratoria, particularly in Texas, after the early-November US midterms).

AI labor displacement is baselined as a temporary rise of about 0.5pp in unemployment, backloaded to 2028-2029, with the US unemployment rate gradually reaching 4.5% and the productivity trend rising to 2.5-3%. GS now sees early signs of broader impact: AI adoption across nonmanufacturing industries correlates significantly negatively with employment growth and positively with unemployment.
Displacement would likely accelerate in a downturn, because the decline in the employment share of routine occupations has been concentrated in recessions.

Inflation should slow in 2027 as tariff pass-through ends (tariffs still add 40bp to year-over-year core PCE through October and drop out next spring), the energy impulse fades and AI-related pressures ease. GS forecasts core PCE falling from 3.2% at end-2026 to 2.4% at end-2027.

Near-term inflation upside risks: remaining energy pass-through (especially European airfares), memory price forecasts revised higher again last earnings season, and broadening upstream cost pressures. The US January effect is a concern, with GS's forecast including a 0.1pp boost to January core PCE.
An adverse Iran scenario would add 0.9pp to 2027 headline inflation and 0.2pp to core relative to baseline.

Fed: GS expects hikes in December and March, one cut in December 2027, then three more cuts in 2028 to a 3.25-3.5% terminal rate. Scenario weights are 50% three hikes then cuts, 35% four hikes with a higher terminal rate, and 15% recession. GS sees more dovish rate risk in the US than elsewhere because the US is most exposed to an AI-cycle downturn.

ECB: final hike in December, with normalization toward a 2.25% terminal rate starting 2027Q4. BoE: final hike to 4.25% in February, a hold for the rest of 2027, cuts to 3.25% starting 2028. GS's ECB and BoE forecasts are dovish relative to market pricing.

Canada: two hikes to 3.0% in 1H27, with the BoC more likely to underdeliver than hike above its neutral range midpoint as the market prices. Australia: RBA hold at 4.85% through October, with 125bp of cumulative cuts by end-2028. Japan is the outlier: BoJ hikes of 25bp in December, March and June to a 2.0% terminal rate, as core CPI is expected above 3.5% through next summer.

EM rate views skew dovish, especially CEEMEA and LatAm, where most central banks are expected to cut through 2027. Asia is flat or slightly higher. GS says markets overestimate EM inflation risk because inflation was low before the shock, EM cycles are weaker than DM, and EM currencies have held up.

Markets are more exposed than the economy to the AI peak. AI has contributed far more to earnings, market value and capex growth than to GDP, and a second-derivative peak often ends the period of positive surprises. AI-infrastructure stocks have derated significantly since June, and S&P 500 earnings are at a record high relative to GDP.

S&P 500 earnings growth is forecast to slow from 36% in 2026 to 11% in 2027. A rotation to hyperscalers, AI-productivity beneficiaries and non-AI companies could cushion the transition. Risks: the market looks ahead to the 2028 investment-share peak, the rotation is slow, a fresh energy spike hits non-AI areas, or financial and credit feedback loops accelerate.

Bonds failed to hedge equities through 2026 because of energy-driven inflation and G10 hikes, with real rates sharply higher over nine months. Near-term risks still push that way (Iran escalation, firm core inflation, Fed commentary). Later in 2027 the risks tilt to lower growth and lower rates, so bonds regain hedging value. GS sees the US 10-year yield at 4.6% at end-2027.

2027 baseline returns: positive for equities and bonds, near zero for commodities. Equity gains should slow well below the 20%+ annualized pace of the last three years. GS recommends overweight US and Japan, neutral Asia ex-Japan/EM, and underweight Europe.

Credit spreads are expected to widen further in 2027 on rising corporate supply, with risks skewed wider. GS expects US HY to underperform, with risk from the tail of weaker borrowers. There is more scope for tightening in Europe.

FX: modest USD weakness as lower inflation and energy weigh on the dollar, with further CNY appreciation on the trade surplus. A sharper shift away from the USD is possible if US tech exceptionalism is challenged, and the same growth risks would likely drive a sharper JPY rise.

Hedging ideas: positioning for lower US and Japan rates or for jointly lower rates and equities, USD/JPY downside, European gas futures and TTF calls for energy upside, and out-of-the-money puts or longer-dated call replacement for equity protection. Equity index volatility is unlikely to fall much and could rise if macro stress broadens.

earnings_insights: GS forecasts S&P 500 earnings growth slowing from 36% in 2026 to 11% in 2027 (GS estimates, not reported figures).
S&P 500 earnings are at a record high relative to GDP. GS says the key question is how much of the profit acceleration persists as the AI investment cycle fades.
Hyperscaler stock reactions to capex signals on earnings calls turned slightly negative in 2026, and upward revisions to hyperscaler capex slowed in the Q3 earnings season.

trade_ideas.description: Buy out-of-the-money equity index puts, or replace equity holdings with longer-dated call options, as equity protection
trade_ideas.rationale: Equity index volatility is more likely to rise than fall, and protection is more valuable as the cycle matures.

trade_ideas.description: Position for lower US and Japan rates, or for jointly lower rates and equities
trade_ideas.rationale: Hedges deeper downside growth tails, and bonds are regaining hedging value.
trade_ideas.risk: Fresh energy shocks or stickier core inflation could push yields higher.

trade_ideas.rationale: USD/JPY generally performs well when rates and equities are both falling.

trade_ideas.description: Buy European gas futures and TTF calls as an energy-upside hedge
trade_ideas.rationale: Asymmetric protection against Iran-related energy price spikes.

trade_ideas.description: Overweight US and Japan equities, neutral Asia ex-Japan/EM, underweight Europe
trade_ideas.rationale: Positive earnings growth and valuation compression support gains, with more US investment resilience.
trade_ideas.risk: AI peak, energy spike or credit feedback loops.

risk_factors: Renewed Iran escalation could push oil to $132/bbl and renew inflation and rate fears.
Bond market turbulence: large fiscal deficits and AI-linked borrowing could lift long-term yields, especially in France.
AI capex disappointment from capacity constraints, regulation, credit market stress or weaker demand.
Earlier or larger AI-related labor market disruption, which would accelerate in a downturn.
Persistence of record US earnings relative to GDP as the AI investment impulse fades.
Wider credit spreads, especially US HY, from heavy AI-linked corporate issuance.
Stickier core inflation from memory prices, upstream costs and the January effect.
vol_and_positioning: Equity index volatility has risen a little but is unlikely to fall much, with scope to rise if macro stresses broaden. The sharpest volatility has been under the surface of the major indices.
Longer-dated options, including out-of-the-money puts or replacing equity holdings with longer-dated calls, look more valuable than usual as the cycle matures.
AI-infrastructure equities have derated significantly since June. Rotation and volatility under the surface could spill into index-level moves.
Hedging ideas: lower US and Japan rates, joint lower rates and equities, USD/JPY downside, and European gas futures and TTF calls for asymmetric protection against energy upside.
geopolitical: War in Iran: renewed escalation, shipping attacks and damage to oil infrastructure could push oil to $132/bbl.
France's fiscal sustainability concerns and the April 2027 presidential and June 2027 parliamentary elections.
US midterm elections in early November raised the possibility of data center permitting moratoria in several states, particularly Texas.
The Democratic victory in November's US election suggests some spending cuts in the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act will be reversed.
US tariff pass-through is ending, and trade uncertainty looms over the BoC outlook.
Japan's Takaichi administration is pursuing consumption tax cuts, higher defense spending and investment plans.

tension_points.bull_case: AI investment still rises strongly in 2027 ($1.1tn to $1.8tn), S&P 500 earnings grow 11%, and the baton passes to hyperscalers, AI-productivity beneficiaries and non-AI companies.
tension_points.bear_case: The market looks ahead to the 2028 investment-share peak, record US earnings relative to GDP prove unsustainable, and capacity constraints, credit stress or regulation cut capex. Equities levered to AI infrastructure have already derated since June.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Capex revisions turning down rather than just slowing, or hyperscaler capex guidance cuts. GS notes upward revisions already slowed in the Q3 earnings season.

tension_points.bull_case: Supply adaptation takes Brent to $78/bbl by end-2027, turning energy into a modest growth tailwind and easing inflation.
tension_points.bear_case: Renewed escalation pushes oil to $132/bbl, adds 0.9pp to headline inflation and hurts equities and bonds.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Escalation with intensified shipping attacks and damage to oil infrastructure.

tension_points.theme: Fed and rates path vs market pricing
tension_points.bull_case: GS expects fewer hikes than priced, a cut in December 2027, and a 10-year yield at 4.6%, which would help both equities and bonds.
tension_points.bear_case: Stickier core inflation, an energy spike or the AI investment impulse could keep yields high, and Fed commentary keeps front-loaded hiking worries alive.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Core inflation surprising to the upside through spring, including a strong January effect.

theme_stances.theme: AI capex peak and market risk
theme_stances.key_argument: AI investment growth stays robust in 2027, so the peak should be manageable for the economy, but markets are more vulnerable to it.

theme_stances.key_argument: Real yields are the highest in many years, and later-2027 risks tilt toward lower growth and lower rates.
theme_stances.evidence: bonds are starting to regain their hedging value
